children: The US federal judiciary is working to develop fresh guidance for judges on the use of generative AI in court operations, with an aim to make new recommendations within the next year, a judge tasked with assessing the emerging technology said on Thursday.

US Circuit Judge Sidney Thomas, the chair of a task force focused on examining AI, expressed confidence in the technology's potential to modernize court operations in comments to reporters after the US Judicial Conference, the judiciary's top policymaking body, met in Washington, D.C.
"Our focus has been effective and safe use of AI," he said.

The 24-member task force identified more than 60 issues for review after it was created last year, including AI's impact on IT security, governance, ethics training, probation, pretrial services, public defender services and cost management.

Thomas said it had made 30 recommendations so far, including guidance to judges nationwide in July 2025 that cautioned against them delegating core judicial functions to AI and recommended they independently verify all AI-generated content.

That guidance has not been released publicly but was detailed in an October letter the judiciary sent to Republican Senator Chuck Grassley, the chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, after two judges acknowledged they used AI to help prepare court orders that contained errors.
Additional recommendations from the task force are expected within the next year, Thomas said, "because we want to wrap up our advisory role and get it onto the conference agenda."

Thomas acknowledged the numerous instances in which judges have discovered AI-generated fictitious case citations and other hallucinated material in court briefs and sanctioned lawyers and litigants representing themselves pro se for that conduct.
But the judge, a member of the San Francisco-based 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals, said he saw promise in AI's potential to streamline court operations and reduce burdens on court personnel.
"We think it can modernize court operations and save a lot of money and improve court operations and ultimately improve the administration of justice," he said.
Thomas pointed to his own court, the nation's largest federal appeals court, where last year 49% of the appeals were pursued by litigants without lawyers, often submitting handwritten filings.

"And we have, with the use of AI, been able to transcribe those pleadings into readable form, which is not only time-saving for the clerks, but also affords the process more access to justice because it assures that their pleadings are actually read and understood," he said.

He said his court and the 5th and 6th US Circuit Courts of Appeals have deployed AI for quality control purposes to review the tens of thousands of briefs they receive each year and ensure they comply with local procedural and formatting rules.

US Circuit Judge Jeffrey Sutton of the 6th Circuit, who chairs the Judicial Conference's executive committee, said that process ensures that clerks' offices can inform litigants they must re-file their briefs and avoid having appeals be dismissed on technical grounds.
"So it's not like AI is ultimately saying no to an appeal," he said. "What it would do is say you've got to correct the brief if you want to submit it. So that's a pretty effective use."
